rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening command to be patient also means to wait: its construction with li carries the sense of awaiting the Lord’s verdict.
rows.anchor: wait) because it is mentioned with the preposition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the sūrah’s end the Prophet is told to remain steadfast and await God’s decision, avoiding Jonah’s impatience.
rows.anchor: being assured to be steadfast and wait for the verdict of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Companion of the fish” affectionately identifies Jonah and evokes the trial he endured.
rows.anchor: There is an element of affection in calling him with this name

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When his people ignored his preaching, Jonah left without God’s permission, was rebuked, and suffered the trial in the fish; the Prophet must not leave his people unless God tells him to.
rows.anchor: he left them without God’s permission; at this, he was rebuked by the Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jonah’s anguished call recalls his immediate recognition of error and repentance, preventing misunderstanding of his folly; God later chose him again.
rows.anchor: He immediately realized his mistake, and in a state of deep anguish

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Lord’s favour was restoring prophethood to Jonah after his repentance was accepted.
rows.anchor: again chose him as a prophet so that he could complete his holy mission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God chose Jonah again to complete his mission; he did not fail in this world but was counted among the righteous and successful.
rows.anchor: he did not fail in this world; he was regarded among the righteous

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is again urged to persevere despite difficult circumstances and accusations; the ending returns to the opening assurance that he is not possessed.
rows.anchor: It is evident that the sūrah ends on the same topic as it began

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the rejecters call the Prophet possessed, the Qur’an remains a reminder to all; they will regret refusing it when regret can no longer help.
rows.anchor: if they do not heed this reminder, they will regret it one day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ma‘ārij complements al-Ḥāqqah: both warn of Judgment and its punishment, with a similar style and a central oath supporting reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: warning people of the Day of Judgement and the punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath also warns arrogant mockers who demand that punishment be hastened; their respite has made them proud, though even a slight divine seizure would humble them.
rows.anchor: the arrogant and haughty people who were making fun of the punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should patiently ignore them for a while because their appointed judgment is near and will show how terrible the punishment they hastened is.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is asked to ignore them for a while; their judgement day is about to arrive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those demanding swift punishment are reprimanded: the torment will certainly come, and no one can avert it.
rows.anchor: this torment shall certainly come upon the disbelievers and no one will be able to avert it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People must not measure God’s timetable by their own; the angels and Gabriel need a day equal to fifty thousand earthly years to reach Him.
rows.anchor: the angels and the Archangel Gabriel need a day which is equal to fifty thousand years

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is urged to be patient because what narrow-minded people regard as far off is near to God.
rows.anchor: what these narrow-minded people are regarding as far-fetched is very near in the eyes of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage depicts cosmic upheaval and the collapse of social bonds; each person would offer even close family and tribe as ransom, while Hell burns and seizes those who evaded the call and hoarded wealth.
rows.anchor: The flames of Hell shall tear and burn his skin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People generally become frustrated and complain when God punishes them even a little for their deeds.
rows.anchor: people generally become frustrated and start complaining if the Almighty punishes them a little

none: publisher-rights notice only; no source commentary

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Jinn complements Sūrah Nūḥ: the prior sūrah showed Noah’s leaders rejecting their messenger, while this one shows the Qur’an moving jinn to spread its message among their kin.
rows.anchor: This sūrah is the counterpart of S ūrah N ūḥ the previous sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn’s encounter is also alluded to in al-Aḥqāf; it is recounted to awaken Quraysh’s honor, since non-addressee jinn were moved while Quraysh turned against the Qur’an and its messenger.
rows.anchor: if the jinn, who are not even the direct addressees of the Qur’ ān could be so deeply moved

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account reassures the Prophet not to grieve over Quraysh’s rejection: dead hearts will not benefit, but even accidental listeners with some capacity for truth can.
rows.anchor: those who even have the slightest ability to appreciate the truth will benefit from it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage addresses Quraysh idolaters, who believed in jinn and maintained a system of soothsaying through contact with them, rather than people who accept only what the senses detect.
rows.anchor: they had also set up a whole system of soothsaying through which they maintained contacts with them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an contrasts soothsayers’ reports from mischievous jinn with this report about righteous jinn, offering Quraysh facts about the unseen that can guide those who discern good from evil.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān has presented before them a report of the righteous among them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Truth-seekers can benefit from these unseen facts; although sense-bound skeptics dismiss them as imagination, providence does not withhold its blessings because some fail to value them.
rows.anchor: providence does not deprive people of its blessings if some unworthy elements fail to recognize and value it

none: translation of Qur’anic verses only; no commentary

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command “tell them” shows that God revealed the jinn’s impressions to the Prophet; they did not narrate them to him directly.
rows.anchor: not narrated to the Prophet (sws) directly from their tongue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A group of jinn happened upon the Prophet while he recited the Qur’an, listened intently, and were moved to call their own people to it.
rows.anchor: They were so moved by it that they intently listened to what was being recited

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The date is uncertain; the author considers this a detailed account of the incident briefly mentioned in al-Aḥqāf and previously discussed its context through reports.
rows.anchor: In my opinion, this is a detailed version of the same incident referred to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has the Prophet convey the report to Quraysh: the Qur’an they disdain deeply affected perceptive jinn, although they were not its direct addressees.
rows.anchor: the same Qur’ ān which they are treating in such a disdainful manner

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Tell them” is meant to awaken Quraysh’s honor and, in passing, to reassure the Prophet that rejection reflects the rejecters’ evil nature, not a flaw in the Book or messenger.
rows.anchor: it is because of their own evil nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn’s announcement was more than praise: recognizing truth and wishing their people well naturally required sharing the divine blessing they had received.
rows.anchor: they did not merely praise the words they heard

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbal noun ʿajab is more emphatic than ʿajīb; it describes the Qur’an’s efficacy, force, wisdom, and beauty, rather than something merely strange.
rows.anchor: In Arabic, this word does not mean “strange”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report implies that jinn know both their own language and the local human language, and that some are connoisseurs of that language.
rows.anchor: the jinn are not only conversant with their own language

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s effectiveness lies in guiding to truth that every good-natured heart can accept; rushd comprehensively names the basic beliefs and virtues innate to human nature.
rows.anchor: this Book is guiding people to the truth which is acceptable to the heart of every good-natured person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If people do not corrupt their nature through misuse of choice or base desires, even a small reminder can restore them to the straight path.
rows.anchor: a little reminder and admonition brings him back on the right track

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawḥīd is the highest form of rushd and the source of basic beliefs and deeds, whose correctness depends on it.
rows.anchor: It is the fountainhead of all basic beliefs and deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn’s sincere profession of faith is the natural obligation that follows from receiving this guidance; tawḥīd rules out associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: It is the natural right of being blessed with this guidance to profess faith in it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Core beliefs and virtues are shared by humans, jinn, and all conscious beings; only social directives differ, while tawḥīd, resurrection, judgment, recompense, and morals are common.
rows.anchor: all basic beliefs and virtues are common not only among all human beings but also the jinn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn explain that tawḥīd forbids attributing a family to God: He is exalted, peerless, and independent, with no wife or children.
rows.anchor: He is solitary and peerless and is not dependent on anything

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word jadd here signifies greatness, grandeur, and high status, conveying God’s unmatched loftiness.
rows.anchor: The implication is that He is so lofty that no one can be His peer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although grammatically the words might attach to the jinn’s “we heard” statement, the author attaches them to “tell them”: the impressions were revealed by God, as are the later statements.
rows.anchor: these impressions of the jinn did not come directly to the Prophet’s knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Safīh means foolish; the jinn apply it to their leader because hearing the Qur’an exposed his foolishness.
rows.anchor: Here, the jinn have used it for their leader because his foolishness became evident to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shataṭ means something that departs from justice and truth.
rows.anchor: means something which does not conform to justice and truth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn recognize their leader’s claims about God’s wife, children, and favored sons and daughters as false, repent, and urge their people not to follow him.
rows.anchor: clearly shows that all these were false allegations concocted by their false leader

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These jinn were common people who had followed their leaders, but faith gave them courage to stop and turn to guidance; Quraysh’s common people are urged to do likewise.
rows.anchor: once the truth became evident to them, they stopped obeying their leaders

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an initially called people in Makka to these innate fundamentals.
rows.anchor: also invited people in the initial period of the Makkan life of the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Through the Prophet, the jinn’s example should help Quraysh’s masses break blind obedience and trust their own judgment.
rows.anchor: they too break the shackles of blindly following their leaders

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn had believed their leaders’ claim that no human or jinn would fabricate false partners and objects of worship for God, but those leaders did exactly that.
rows.anchor: they thought that men or jinn could never impute such falsities to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn warn their people against blind trust in religious authorities and urge them to use their own senses to avoid serious loss.
rows.anchor: they should not blindly follow their religious pundits

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahq literally means burdening someone beyond what they can bear, then extends to sin, oppression, cruelty, or usurping rights; verse 13 uses it for injustice.
rows.anchor: real meaning of the word

rows.speaker: people
rows.claim: A common interpretation says foolish humans sought refuge with jinn and thereby made the jinn arrogant and supercilious.
rows.anchor: Generally, people have interpreted this verse to mean that some foolish human beings took refuge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects that interpretation because it contributes no useful information and stretches rahq beyond its basic meaning.
rows.anchor: This interpretation does not seem to be correct

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He instead parses the humans as increasing the jinn’s rebellion: humans sought jinn protection from calamities, but the jinn drew them into the evil rather than protecting them.
rows.anchor: some foolish men sought refuge with the jinn so that they could save them from calamities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab idolaters treated jinn as sources of unseen knowledge, enabling a deceptive soothsaying system that claimed sacrifices or vows could avert an angry jinn’s harm.
rows.anchor: a whole system of soothsaying which was totally based on lies and deception

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Soothsayers sometimes instructed credulous people to sacrifice even their children to appease jinn.
rows.anchor: foolish people at the behest of these soothsayers would at times even

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another Arab superstition assigned particular jinn to each valley and mountain, requiring travelers to seek the local chief’s protection against calamity; this imposed needless burdens.
rows.anchor: every valley and every mountain was inhabited by some specific group of jinn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pious jinn refer to these superstitions to show that deficient understanding of tawḥīd had joined foolish humans with mischievous jinn, producing spiritual and material evils the Qur’an came to uproot.
rows.anchor: an alliance has come into being between some foolish human beings and some mischievous jinn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite rijāl can magnify or belittle; readings include foolish humans with foolish jinn or mischievous humans with mischievous jinn, and the author says Arabic permits foolish humans seeking mischievous jinn.
rows.anchor: it would be totally in accordance with the principles of Arabic if this verse is interpreted thus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After tawḥīd, the jinn identify resurrection denial shared by jinn and humans; dispelling it is one purpose of the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: the jinn have now pointed out the misconceptions of both groups – humankind and jinnkind – regarding the Hereafter

rows.speaker: people
rows.claim: Some interpreters understand the verse to say that both jinn and humans wrongly thought God would send no further prophet.
rows.anchor: Some people have interpreted this verse differently

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the wording could support the alternative, but questions it because the Qur’an’s primary audience was awaiting a prophet, as he explains next.
rows.anchor: Although the words of this verse can be interpreted thus, however a question arises on it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an’s primary audiences awaited a prophet: earlier predictions were hidden by the People of the Book but could not be denied, and even the unlettered Ishmaelites did not firmly deny the expectation.
rows.anchor: were waiting for a prophet because of prediction made by earlier prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Before the Prophet’s advent the Ishmaelites claimed they would be first to accept a prophet from among them, but became his opponents when God sent him; this supports resurrection rather than prophethood as the verse’s subject.
rows.anchor: they would be the first ones to accept him and the ones to follow his guidance the most

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn report that, at the Qur’an’s revelation, the heavens were newly filled with guards and meteors; Qur’anic reports of devils being pelted while eavesdropping are confirmed by this experience, though access had previously been possible.
rows.anchor: This personal experience of the jinn substantiates this information

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At that time the guards and meteors prevented jinn from entering the surveillance system to eavesdrop on the unseen.
rows.anchor: the heavens were filled with meteors and sentinels to such an extent that the jinn were not able to infiltrate the system

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn could not explain the cosmic change; the next verse says they did not know its wisdom, though their linkage of it to Qur’an’s revelation implied a connection.
rows.anchor: they were unaware of the wisdom behind what was happening

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author agrees with their deduction: divine surveillance was made especially rigorous at the Qur’an’s revelation to protect it from incursions, while the system had always operated and devils had been pelted even before.
rows.anchor: the system of surveillance which the Almighty has set up in this universe to stop the jinn from intervening in divine matters became very rigorous
